stem: According to the graph, how many years after the survey began did the trout population reach its maximum?
stimulus: Ecologists counted the brook trout in a restored mountain pond once a month after stocking ended. The graph models the trout population $P$ as a function of $t$, the number of months since the survey began.

figure.caption: Brook Trout Population in a Restored Pond
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts at (0, 80), rises to a highest point at (18, 260), and falls back to (36, 80).

explanation: The maximum is the highest point of the curve, its vertex. Follow it down to the horizontal axis: the vertex is at t = 18. The axis counts months, but the question asks for years, so divide by 12: 18 ÷ 12 = 1.5 years.

common_errors.why: Read the vertex's t-coordinate correctly in months but did not convert to years.
Gave the maximum population, the vertex's y-coordinate, instead of the time it happens.
Converted 36 months, the end of the graph, to years instead of the vertex time.
Converted 260 instead of 18 (260 ÷ 12) after swapping the vertex coordinates.

stem: According to the model, what is the maximum average weekly earnings, in dollars?
stimulus: A labour economist modelled how the average weekly earnings of warehouse supervisors change over a career. In the graph, $x$ is years of work experience and $E$ is average weekly earnings in hundreds of dollars.

figure.caption: Average Weekly Earnings by Years of Experience
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts at (0, 6), rises to a highest point at (20, 14), and falls to (40, 6).

explanation: The maximum is the vertex, the highest point of the curve. It is at (20, 14), so the greatest value of E is 14. The vertical axis is in hundreds of dollars, so 14 hundred dollars is 14 × 100 = 1400 dollars.

common_errors.why: Read the vertex height correctly but did not convert hundreds of dollars to dollars.
Gave the vertex's x-coordinate (years of experience) instead of the earnings.
Took the x-coordinate 20 and applied the hundreds conversion to it.
Read the y-intercept (starting earnings, 6 hundred dollars) instead of the maximum.
Read the y-intercept and did not convert it either.

stem: According to the graph, what is the minimum average response time, in milliseconds?
stimulus: In a word-recognition experiment, linguists showed participants written words from 2 to 12 letters long and timed how quickly each participant decided whether the word was real. The graph models the average response time $R$, in milliseconds, as a function of word length $x$, in letters.

figure.caption: Average Response Time by Word Length
figure.alt: An upward-opening parabola that starts at (2, 575), falls to a lowest point at (7, 475), and rises back to (12, 575).

explanation: The minimum is the lowest point of the curve, its vertex, at x = 7. Go across from that point to the vertical axis. That axis starts at 400, not 0, and each gridline adds 25, so the vertex is three gridlines up: 400 + 3 × 25 = 475 milliseconds.

common_errors.why: Gave the vertex's x-coordinate (word length) instead of the response time.
Counted three gridlines above 400 but assumed each gridline is 10 instead of 25.
Assumed the vertical axis starts at 0 and counted only the three gridlines of 25.
Read the highest value shown, at either end of the graph, instead of the lowest.

stem: According to the graph, how many meters does the stone rise between leaving the sling and reaching its greatest height?
stimulus: To test how ancient slingers could hit hilltop targets, a team of experimental archaeologists filmed a replica clay sling stone in flight. The graph models the stone's height $h$, in meters above the ground, $t$ seconds after it left the sling, for the first 4 seconds of flight.

figure.caption: Height of a Replica Sling Stone
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts at (0, 4), rises to a highest point at (2, 24), and falls back to (4, 4).

explanation: You need two points. The stone leaves the sling at t = 0, so its starting height is the y-intercept: 4 meters. Its greatest height is the vertex, the top of the curve: 24 meters at t = 2. The stone rises 24 − 4 = 20 meters.

common_errors.why: Gave the maximum height measured from the ground, not the rise from the launch height.
Gave the launch height (the y-intercept) instead of the rise.
Gave the time of the vertex instead of a height.
Added the launch height to the maximum height instead of subtracting it.
Took the starting height as 2, swapping in the vertex's t-coordinate, and computed 24 − 2.

stem: According to the graph, what was the greatest number of temporary workers the agency placed in a single week?
stimulus: A labour economist tracked a staffing agency's placements during a 12-week hiring season. The graph shows the number of temporary workers placed, in hundreds, $x$ weeks after the season opened.

figure.caption: Temporary Workers Placed per Week
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts at the origin, rises to a highest point at x = 6, and falls back to the x-axis at x = 12.

explanation: "Greatest number" means the highest point on the curve, which is the vertex. Follow it across to the vertical axis: it sits at 45, with the gridlines going up in 5s. But the axis counts workers in hundreds, so 45 hundreds is 45 × 100 = 4,500 workers.

common_errors.why: Read the vertex correctly but never converted from hundreds to workers.
Gave the week when the peak happens (the x-coordinate) rather than how many workers were placed.
Took the x-coordinate of the vertex and multiplied it by 100.
Counted 9 gridlines up to the peak as if each one were 1, then multiplied by 100.

stem: At what depth, in meters, does the fern spore count reach its minimum?
stimulus: A paleobotanist counted fossil fern spores in a sediment core. The graph shows the count, in spores per gram of sediment, at a depth of $x$ meters below the top of the core.

figure.caption: Fern Spores in a Sediment Core
figure.alt: An upward-opening parabola that starts at 44 on the vertical axis, falls to a lowest point at x = 8, and rises back to 44 at x = 16.

explanation: The minimum is the lowest point on the curve, the vertex. The question asks for a depth, which is on the horizontal axis. Drop straight down from the lowest point to the x-axis. The gridlines go up in 2s, so the vertex is 4 gridlines along, at 8 meters.

common_errors.why: Gave the smallest spore count (the y-coordinate of the vertex) rather than the depth where it happens.
Counted 4 gridlines along to the vertex and treated each one as 1 meter when they go up in 2s.
Read the y-intercept, the spore count at the top of the core, instead of the lowest point.
Gave the deepest point shown on the graph instead of where the count bottoms out.

stem: According to the graph, what is the predicted corn yield, in bushels per acre, for a plot that receives no nitrogen fertilizer?
stimulus: An agricultural scientist modeled corn yield as a function of the amount of nitrogen fertilizer applied. The graph shows the predicted yield for $x$ pounds of nitrogen per acre.

figure.caption: Predicted Corn Yield and Nitrogen Applied
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts on the vertical axis, rises to a highest point at x = 80, and falls back to the same height at x = 160.

explanation: No nitrogen means x = 0, so you want the y-intercept, where the curve meets the vertical axis. The vertical gridlines go up in 8s. The curve meets the axis 7 gridlines up, which is 7 × 8 = 56 bushels per acre.

common_errors.why: Read the maximum yield (the vertex) instead of the yield at x = 0.
Gave the amount of nitrogen that gives the highest yield, the x-coordinate of the vertex.
Counted 7 gridlines up to the y-intercept and treated each as 1 when they go up in 8s.
Read the x-value of the point (0 pounds of nitrogen) instead of the yield there.

stem: How far east of the western end of the transect, in kilometers, is the highest point of the hill?
stimulus: A cartographer drew an elevation profile along a straight east–west transect across a hill. The graph shows the elevation, in meters, at a point $x$ kilometers east of the transect's western end.

figure.caption: Elevation Profile Across a Hill
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola that starts low on the vertical axis, rises to a highest point midway across, and falls back to the same height at x = 7.

explanation: The highest point of the hill is the vertex of the curve. The question asks how far east, so you want its x-coordinate. Drop straight down from the peak to the horizontal axis. The gridlines there go up in 0.5s, and the peak is 7 gridlines along, at 3.5 km.

common_errors.why: Counted 7 gridlines along to the peak and treated each as 1 km when they go up in 0.5s.
Gave the hill's maximum elevation (the y-coordinate of the vertex) instead of its distance east.
Read the elevation where the curve meets the vertical axis (the y-intercept) instead of the peak.

stem: According to the graph, what is the minimum height, in meters, of the cable above the deck?

figure.alt: An upward-opening parabola that starts on the vertical axis at the left tower, dips to a lowest point midway between the towers, and rises back to the same height at x = 100.

explanation: Minimum height means the lowest point of the cable, which is the vertex of the curve. The question asks for a height, so read the vertex across on the vertical axis. The gridlines go up in 10s, and the lowest point sits on the first one, at 10 meters.

common_errors.why: Gave the distance from the left tower where the lowest point is (the x-coordinate of the vertex) instead of the height.
Read the height at the towers, the y-intercept, instead of the lowest point.
Counted 1 gridline up to the vertex and treated it as 1 meter when the gridlines go up in 10s.
Took the deck level (the x-axis) as the cable's lowest point without reading the curve.

stem: According to the model, how many million years after the start of the record did the number of fern species reach its maximum?
stimulus: A paleobotanist modeled the number of fern species found in a sequence of fossil beds, $S$, as a function of time $t$, in millions of years after the start of the fossil record. The graph of the model is shown.

figure.caption: Fern species in a fossil record
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola over 0 to 12 million years that rises to a single highest point and then falls.

explanation: A maximum is the highest turning point of the curve, which is the vertex. Follow the vertex straight down to the horizontal axis. Each gridline on that axis is 2 million years, so the vertex is at t = 6. The question asks when the maximum happened, not how many species there were, so the answer is the t-coordinate: 6.

common_errors.why: Gave the maximum number of species (the vertex's S-coordinate) instead of the time when it happened.
Counted the vertex as the 3rd gridline and forgot that the time axis goes up in steps of 2.

stem: According to the model, what was the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, at midnight?
stimulus: A meteorologist modeled the air temperature at a weather station during one night, $T$, in degrees Fahrenheit, as a function of $h$, the number of hours after midnight. The graph of the model is shown.

figure.caption: Overnight temperature at a weather station
figure.alt: An upward-opening parabola over 0 to 12 hours that falls to a single lowest point and then rises.

explanation: Midnight is 0 hours after midnight, so you want the point where h = 0, which is the T-intercept. Find where the curve starts on the vertical axis, then count up from 30 in steps of 2. The curve starts at 50, so the temperature at midnight was 50°F.

common_errors.why: Read the lowest temperature (the vertex) instead of the temperature at h = 0.
Gave the time of the minimum (the vertex's h-coordinate) instead of a temperature.
Counted 10 gridlines up from the bottom and didn't convert, ignoring that the axis starts at 30 and goes up in 2s.

figure.caption: Height of a served volleyball
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola from 0 to 3 seconds that rises to a single highest point and then falls.

explanation: The maximum height is the vertex, the highest point of the curve. Read across from the vertex to the vertical axis, which counts in 4s. The vertex is level with 40, so the ball's maximum height is 40 feet.

common_errors.why: Gave the time when the maximum happens instead of the height.
Read the starting height (the y-intercept) instead of the highest point.

stem: According to the model, how many birds were in the colony at the start of the study?
stimulus: An ornithologist modeled the number of breeding terns in a colony, $P$, in hundreds of birds, as a function of $x$, the number of years since a study began. The graph of the model is shown.

figure.caption: Tern colony size
figure.alt: A decreasing curve over 0 to 10 years that starts high on the vertical axis and flattens toward zero.

explanation: The start of the study is x = 0, so you want the P-intercept. The curve meets the vertical axis at 12. That axis is measured in hundreds of birds, so 12 hundred is 1,200 birds.

common_errors.why: Read the intercept correctly but ignored that the axis is in hundreds of birds.
Counted the intercept as the 6th gridline without using the axis step of 2.
Counted 6 gridlines and converted to hundreds, but missed the step of 2.

stem: The graph of $y = f(x)$ has its vertex at $(h, k)$. What is the value of $h + k$?
stimulus: An ecologist modeled the number of mayfly nymphs per square meter of streambed, $f(x)$, as a function of the water temperature $x$, in degrees Celsius. The graph of $y = f(x)$ is shown.

figure.caption: Mayfly nymphs and water temperature
figure.alt: A downward-opening parabola over 0 to 24 degrees Celsius that rises to a single highest point and then falls.

explanation: The vertex is the turning point, which here is the highest point of the curve. Read it in two parts. Go down to the temperature axis, which counts in 2s: h = 12. Go across to the vertical axis, which counts in 10s: k = 90. Then h + k = 12 + 90 = 102.

common_errors.why: Read k and stopped without adding h.
Read h and stopped without adding k.
Counted the vertex as the 6th gridline on the temperature axis, forgetting that it goes up in 2s, so used h = 6.

stem: According to the model, in what year was the number of performances at its minimum?
stimulus: A musicologist modeled the average number of performances per year of a little-known string quartet, $N$, as a function of $d$, the number of decades after 1900. The graph of the model is shown.

figure.caption: Performances of a string quartet
figure.alt: An upward-opening parabola over 0 to 10 decades that falls to a single lowest point and then rises.

explanation: The minimum is the lowest point of the curve, which is the vertex. Its d-coordinate is 5. That means 5 decades, or 50 years, after 1900, so the year is 1900 + 50 = 1950.

common_errors.why: Read d = 5 correctly but didn't convert decades after 1900 into a year.
Gave the minimum number of performances (the vertex's N-coordinate) instead of when it happened.
Treated d as years instead of decades and added 5 to 1900.
